zufft for scipy.fft users

Source: vignettes/articles/zufft-for-scipy-users.Rmd
zufft-for-scipy-users.Rmd

zufft runs the same ducc0 code as scipy.fft, with the same definitions, normalisations and fast lengths, so spectra computed in R and in Python agree to rounding. The test suite checks this against 2040 SciPy reference cases.

library(zufft)

Names

scipy.fft zufft
fft(x, n, axis) fft_c2c(x, n = n, axes = axis + 1)
ifft fft_c2c(..., inverse = TRUE)
fft2, fftn(x, s, axes) fft_c2c(x, n = s, axes = axes + 1)
rfft, rfft2, rfftn fft_r2c()
irfft, irfft2, irfftn fft_c2r()
dct, dctn fft_dct()
idct, idctn fft_dct(..., inverse = TRUE)
dst, dstn, idst, idstn fft_dst()
fftfreq, rfftfreq fft_freq(), fft_rfreq()
fftshift, ifftshift fft_shift(), fft_ishift()
next_fast_len, prev_fast_len fft_next_len(), fft_prev_len()
get_workers, set_workers fft_workers(), with_fft_workers()

hfft, ihfft, the fast Hankel transform, the backend machinery and overwrite_x are not offered.

Axes

Axes are 1-based in R. NumPy axis k is R axis k + 1, and an array moved between R and NumPy by reticulate keeps its shape, so the mapping is the same for every array.

The default differs: SciPy’s 1-D functions use the last axis, while zufft’s axes = NULL means every axis, as stats::fft() does. A 1-D SciPy call on a matrix is therefore axes = 2 here:

m <- matrix(1:6, 2)
fft_c2c(m, axes = 2)   # scipy.fft.fft(m) along the last axis
#>       [,1]         [,2]         [,3]
#> [1,]  9+0i -3+1.732051i -3-1.732051i
#> [2,] 12+0i -3+1.732051i -3-1.732051i

n takes one value per transformed axis and is never recycled; SciPy’s rule that a short s selects the trailing axes does not apply.

Normalisation

norm has SciPy’s three values, with the same meaning: "backward" (the default) scales the inverse by 1/N, "forward" the forward transform, and "ortho" both by 1/sqrt(N). zufft adds "none", which scales neither, as FFTW and stats::fft() do.

x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2)
fft_dct(x, norm = "ortho")
#> [1]  6.123724e+00 -1.115355e+00 -2.000000e+00  4.082483e-01 -1.110223e-16
#> [6] -2.988585e-01

For the cosine and sine transforms, orthogonalize defaults to norm == "ortho", as in SciPy. Like SciPy, zufft ignores an explicit orthogonalize for complex input.

Speed in R

R stores arrays column by column, so the contiguous axis is the first, where in NumPy it is the last. The real transforms halve the last axis you list, as SciPy does. Listing the first axis last halves the contiguous axis and is often much faster:

m <- matrix(rnorm(512 * 512), 512)
dim(fft_r2c(m))            # SciPy's order: halves axis 2
#> [1] 512 257
dim(fft_r2c(m, axes = 2:1)) # halves axis 1, the fast one in R
#> [1] 257 512
